items.stem: Which term describes broad agreement among members of a society about its main values and goals?
items.answer: Value consensus
items.markingKey: Value consensus: broad agreement among members of a society about its main values and goals. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “functional prerequisites”? Give one example.
items.answer: The basic needs that every society must meet in order to survive. Example: Parsons’s four needs: adaptation, goal attainment, integration and latency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the basic needs that every society must meet in order to survive); 1 mark for a relevant example such as Parsons’s four needs: adaptation, goal attainment, integration and latency. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “latent function” and “manifest function”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Latent function: an unintended and often unrecognised consequence of an institution or practice (e.g. schools providing childcare that allows parents to work). Manifest function: the intended and recognised consequence of an institution or practice (e.g. a school teaching pupils to read and write).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: In Manila, a national holiday brings families and communities together in shared ceremonies and celebrations. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: society is built up from small-scale interactions in which people create shared meanings, negotiate roles and apply labels; the situation should be understood through the meanings the people involved give to it (Mead, Blumer, Becker).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: After a factory closes in a small town near Nairobi, crime and suicide rates rise and people say they no longer know “what the rules are”. Explain how postmodernist and functionalist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: society is fragmented and diverse; there are no fixed structures or single truths, so individuals choose identities and lifestyles from many options and the situation reflects choice, consumption and media-saturated culture (Lyotard, Baudrillard). Functionalism: society is a system of interdependent institutions that meet needs (functional prerequisites); shared norms and values (value consensus) learnt through socialisation create social order and integration, so the situation can be seen as contributing to stability (Durkheim, Parsons).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: After a factory closes in a small town near Kathmandu, crime and suicide rates rise and people say they no longer know “what the rules are”. Compare how Marxist and functionalist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: society is based on conflict between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat; institutions spread ruling-class ideology and false class consciousness, so the situation reflects and reproduces class inequality and exploitation (Marx, Althusser). Functionalism: society is a system of interdependent institutions that meet needs (functional prerequisites); shared norms and values (value consensus) learnt through socialisation create social order and integration, so the situation can be seen as contributing to stability (Durkheim, Parsons).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of participant observation for studying how far young people in Madrid share the same values as their parents.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; it is flexible and can uncover issues the researcher had not anticipated. Limitations: it cannot measure the extent of a pattern across a whole society; studies are small-scale and impossible to repeat exactly, so findings are unreliable and hard to generalise. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far young people in Madrid share the same values as their parents but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating how far young people in Seoul share the same values as their parents. Evaluate the use of official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do; interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how far young people in Seoul share the same values as their parents but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “organic analogy”?
items.answer: The comparison of society to a living body whose parts (institutions) each perform a function for the whole.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the comparison of society to a living body whose parts (institutions) each perform a function for the whole. [1]

items.stem: Which term describes the capitalist ruling class who own the means of production?
items.answer: Bourgeoisie
items.markingKey: Bourgeoisie: the capitalist ruling class who own the means of production. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “proletariat”, and give one example.
items.answer: The working class who must sell their labour power to the bourgeoisie in order to survive. Example: factory and service workers paid wages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the working class who must sell their labour power to the bourgeoisie in order to survive); 1 mark for a relevant example such as factory and service workers paid wages. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “hegemony” and “false class consciousness”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Hegemony: the ideological leadership of the ruling class, which wins the consent of the subordinate class (e.g. popular media presenting capitalism as the only realistic system). False class consciousness: a state in which the working class accepts ruling-class ideas and fails to recognise its own exploitation (e.g. workers believing that inequality is natural and fair).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A large company in Dhaka announces record profits while cutting the wages of its warehouse workers. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: society is built up from small-scale interactions in which people create shared meanings, negotiate roles and apply labels; the situation should be understood through the meanings the people involved give to it (Mead, Blumer, Becker).

items.stem: Workers at a clothing factory near Lima go on strike after a fire reveals unsafe working conditions. Explain how radical feminist and Marxist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: society is patriarchal: men dominate women in every sphere, including the family and personal relationships, so the situation is an example of male power and the oppression of women (Firestone, Millett). Marxism: society is based on conflict between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat; institutions spread ruling-class ideology and false class consciousness, so the situation reflects and reproduces class inequality and exploitation (Marx, Althusser).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating changes in income inequality over the last thirty years. Evaluate the use of longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they are ideal for tracking change in the same individuals or families over many years; comparing the same people at different points avoids the problem of comparing different samples. Limitations: they are very expensive and results take many years to appear; being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in income inequality over the last thirty years but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using field experiments to research workers’ attitudes towards their employers in a large factory.
items.answer: Strengths: they take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory; participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally. Limitations: the researcher has much less control over variables than in a laboratory; they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying workers’ attitudes towards their employers in a large factory but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Define the term “liberal feminism”, and give one example.
items.answer: The feminist view that gender inequality can be reduced through reforms such as equal opportunities laws and changes in socialisation. Example: campaigns for equal pay legislation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the feminist view that gender inequality can be reduced through reforms such as equal opportunities laws and changes in socialisation); 1 mark for a relevant example such as campaigns for equal pay legislation. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “patriarchy” and “radical feminism”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Patriarchy: a social system in which men hold power and dominate women (e.g. male control of political leadership and household decisions). Radical feminism: the feminist view that patriarchy is the main and most universal form of inequality and must be overthrown (e.g. arguing that the family and sexual relationships are sites of male power).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A survey in Madrid finds that women hold only one in five senior management posts in large companies, although they make up half of the workforce. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: different roles for men and women may be seen as functional: Parsons argued instrumental (male) and expressive (female) roles complement each other and help the family meet society’s needs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In a dual-earner household in Accra, both partners work full-time but Lucas’s wife still does most of the cooking, cleaning and childcare. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: the situation is an example of patriarchy, the system of male domination found in all societies; men benefit from women’s labour and subordination, and only radical change will end it (Firestone, Walby).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Freya, a sociology student, is designing a project on gender stereotypes in children’s play. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying gender stereotypes in children’s play but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes an approach that explains society through the meanings and motives behind individuals’ actions?
items.answer: Social action theory
items.markingKey: Social action theory: an approach that explains society through the meanings and motives behind individuals’ actions. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “labelling”? Give one example.
items.answer: The process of attaching a definition or name to a person, which may shape how others treat them. Example: a teacher calling a pupil a “troublemaker”.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the process of attaching a definition or name to a person, which may shape how others treat them); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a teacher calling a pupil a “troublemaker”. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “looking-glass self” and “definition of the situation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Looking-glass self: Cooley’s idea that our self-image develops from how we think others see us (e.g. a teenager deciding they are clever because teachers praise them). Definition of the situation: the meaning people give to a situation, which shapes how they act in it (e.g. treating a rumour of a bank collapse as true and withdrawing savings).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: At a new school in Madrid, Jonas is seated at the back of the class and called “lazy” by a teacher in the first week; by the end of term Jonas has stopped handing in homework. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: society is based on conflict between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat; institutions spread ruling-class ideology and false class consciousness, so the situation reflects and reproduces class inequality and exploitation (Marx, Althusser).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A young man in Mexico City who has been released from prison finds that employers reject him as soon as they learn about his conviction. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: society is patriarchal: men dominate women in every sphere, including the family and personal relationships, so the situation is an example of male power and the oppression of women (Firestone, Millett).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful self-completion questionnaires are for studying everyday impression management in the workplace.
items.answer: Strengths: there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying everyday impression management in the workplace but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “pick and mix identity”, and give one example.
items.answer: An identity constructed by choosing from a range of cultural options rather than inherited from class or tradition. Example: a young person combining fashion, music and religion from several cultures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (an identity constructed by choosing from a range of cultural options rather than inherited from class or tradition); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a young person combining fashion, music and religion from several cultures. [2]

items.stem: A survey in Nairobi finds that fewer young people describe themselves as “working class” or “middle class”, and more describe themselves through hobbies, brands and online communities. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identity is now chosen and fluid; consumption, media and globalisation allow pick-and-mix identities, so fixed categories such as class matter less (Lyotard, Baudrillard).

items.stem: Ethan is planning a study of how far young people in Cape Town share the same values as their parents. Explain two strengths of using non-participant observation for this research.
items.answer: 1. It records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts. 2. A structured observation schedule allows behaviour to be counted and compared, improving reliability.

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of agreement with shared social values (240 adults, Mexico City). Table: percentage agreeing that “most people share the same basic values” | 2005 | 2025. Aged 18-34 | 55% | 40%. Aged 35-54 | 68% | 59%. Aged 55+ | 72% | 73%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Aged 18-34 between 2005 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that modern societies are still based on value consensus.
items.answer: (a) (40 − 55) ÷ 55 × 100 = -27.3%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Aged 55+; the figure fell for Aged 18-34, Aged 35-54; Aged 55+ had the highest figure for 2025. Older people were socialised when communities and religion were stronger, so they perceive more consensus. Qualifications: Even if majorities agree, falling figures for younger people suggest growing diversity; Marxists would add that apparent agreement may reflect ruling-class ideology rather than genuine consensus. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 240 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (40 − 55) ÷ 55 × 100; 1 mark for -27.3% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain Gramsci’s argument that the ruling class maintains power mainly through hegemony, winning consent rather than using force, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Gramsci argued that the working class can develop counter-hegemonic ideas through “organic intellectuals”, so ideology can be resisted. Criticism: Some argue it is hard to measure hegemony and that consent may simply reflect genuinely shared values.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Ravi, a sociology student, is designing a project on changes in income inequality over the last thirty years. Explain one strength of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified.

items.stem: A sociologist in Nairobi wants to research how far people accept inequality as fair. Explain two limitations of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. They are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. 2. The interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how far people accept inequality as fair. [4]

items.stem: A survey of 1000 workers in Seoul produced the data below. Table: percentage agreeing that “in this country, people get rewarded for their effort and skill” | 2000 | 2025. Manual workers | 50% | 46%. Routine non-manual workers | 49% | 51%. Professionals and managers | 73% | 76%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Professionals and managers between 2000 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that most people accept ruling-class ideology.
items.answer: (a) (76 − 73) ÷ 73 × 100 = 4.1%. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Routine non-manual workers, Professionals and managers; the figure fell for Manual workers; Professionals and managers had the highest figure for 2025. Growing inequality and insecure work may be weakening false class consciousness among manual workers. Qualifications: Large and possibly growing minorities reject the idea that rewards are fair, suggesting class consciousness and resistance; figures may reflect real differences in experience rather than ideology. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 1000 workers in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (76 − 73) ÷ 73 × 100; 1 mark for 4.1% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Oakley argued that the housewife role is socially constructed and oppressive rather than natural. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Oakley’s interviews with London housewives found most were dissatisfied with housework, which was monotonous and isolating; she argued gender roles are learnt through socialisation (manipulation and canalisation). Criticism: Radical feminists argue reform of socialisation is not enough because patriarchy is structural.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Liberal feminism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating women’s experiences of the dual burden. Explain one strength of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of women’s experiences of the dual burden. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using covert participant observation to research women’s experiences of the dual burden.
items.answer: Strengths: it produces rich, first-hand qualitative data with high validity; it can give access to closed or deviant groups who would refuse an overt researcher. Limitations: the researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered; note-taking is difficult, so data depends on memory and may be inaccurate. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying women’s experiences of the dual burden but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “verstehen”.

items.stem: Explain Cooley’s argument that the self is a “looking-glass self”, formed by imagining how others see us, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Cooley argued people imagine how they appear to others, imagine others’ judgements and develop feelings about themselves accordingly. Criticism: It may overstate how far people accept others’ views; people can resist negative labels.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful covert participant observation is for studying the importance of social class to people’s sense of identity.
items.answer: Strengths: it produces rich, first-hand qualitative data with high validity; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: it involves deception and lack of informed consent, which breaks ethical guidelines; the researcher may be drawn into illegal or harmful activity and is at risk if discovered. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the importance of social class to people’s sense of identity but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).

items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Parsons’s AGIL model links each need to a sub-system (economy, polity, religion/law, family/education); value consensus integrates the system. [2]

items.stem: A research team is investigating participation in religious and national ceremonies. Explain one limitation of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: They show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of participation in religious and national ceremonies. [2]

items.stem: A school in Nairobi holds a weekly assembly where pupils sing the national anthem and celebrate pupils who have worked hard. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: society is based on conflict between the bourgeoisie, who own the means of production, and the proletariat; institutions spread ruling-class ideology and false class consciousness, so the situation reflects and reproduces class inequality and exploitation (Marx, Althusser).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Chloe is planning a study of the effects of rapid economic change on community life. Evaluate the use of laboratory experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability; results are quantitative and easy to compare. Limitations: it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour; many social issues cannot be studied in a laboratory for ethical or practical reasons. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of rapid economic change on community life but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the resources used to produce goods and wealth, such as land, factories, machinery and capital?
items.answer: Means of production
items.markingKey: Means of production: the resources used to produce goods and wealth, such as land, factories, machinery and capital. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “bourgeoisie” and “proletariat”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Bourgeoisie: the capitalist ruling class who own the means of production (e.g. owners of factories, banks and large companies). Proletariat: the working class who must sell their labour power to the bourgeoisie in order to survive (e.g. factory and service workers paid wages).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A large company in Nairobi announces record profits while cutting the wages of its warehouse workers. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: society is fragmented and diverse; there are no fixed structures or single truths, so individuals choose identities and lifestyles from many options and the situation reflects choice, consumption and media-saturated culture (Lyotard, Baudrillard).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Workers at a clothing factory near Riyadh go on strike after a fire reveals unsafe working conditions. Explain how a radical feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Radical feminism: society is patriarchal: men dominate women in every sphere, including the family and personal relationships, so the situation is an example of male power and the oppression of women (Firestone, Millett).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A research team is investigating changes in income inequality over the last thirty years. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised. Limitations: they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying changes in income inequality over the last thirty years but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the feminist view that gender inequality can be reduced through reforms such as equal opportunities laws and changes in socialisation?
items.answer: Liberal feminism
items.markingKey: Liberal feminism: the feminist view that gender inequality can be reduced through reforms such as equal opportunities laws and changes in socialisation. [1]

items.stem: Explain two differences between liberal and radical feminism.
items.answer: Liberal feminists see inequality as caused by socialisation and discrimination and seek gradual reform through laws and policies; radical feminists see patriarchy as the root of all inequality, embedded in the family and sexuality, and seek revolutionary change, sometimes separatism.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained difference (cause of inequality; solution/strategy). [4]

items.stem: In a dual-earner household in Colombo, both partners work full-time but Jonas’s wife still does most of the cooking, cleaning and childcare. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: different roles for men and women may be seen as functional: Parsons argued instrumental (male) and expressive (female) roles complement each other and help the family meet society’s needs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of gender and senior employment (250 large companies, Mexico City). Table: percentage of senior management posts held | 2010 | 2025. Women | 18% | 28%. Men | 80% | 77%. (a) Suppose 200 of the respondents were Men. Using the 2025 figure, calculate how many of them gave this response. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of gender and senior employment. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that gender inequality in employment is disappearing.
items.answer: (a) 77% of 200 = 77 ÷ 100 × 200 = 154 (to the nearest whole person). (b) Definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Women; the figure fell for Men; Men had the highest figure for 2025. Marxist feminists would argue women are used as a flexible reserve army of labour in lower-paid roles. Qualifications: Women still hold a minority of senior posts; pay gaps, part-time work and the dual burden continue, as radical and Marxist feminists argue. The data also come from official statistics of 250 large companies in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method (77 ÷ 100 × 200); 1 mark answer 154. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: State one reason why interactionists prefer qualitative research methods.
items.answer: They want to understand meanings, which requires verstehen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. they want to understand meanings, which requires verstehen. [1]

items.stem: Explain two criticisms of interactionism.
items.answer: It neglects wider social structures and power such as class and patriarchy; it is hard to generalise from its small-scale studies; it can be too deterministic about labels, ignoring resistance; it does not explain where labels originate.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Staff at a restaurant in Accra are polite and cheerful to customers but joke and complain about them in the kitchen. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: society is a system of interdependent institutions that meet needs (functional prerequisites); shared norms and values (value consensus) learnt through socialisation create social order and integration, so the situation can be seen as contributing to stability (Durkheim, Parsons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: State one feature of postmodern society.
items.answer: Fragmentation and cultural diversity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. fragmentation and cultural diversity. [1]

items.stem: Kenji, a teenager in Dhaka, mixes K-pop music, streetwear from the USA, traditional family festivals and an online gaming identity. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: identity is now chosen and fluid; consumption, media and globalisation allow pick-and-mix identities, so fixed categories such as class matter less (Lyotard, Baudrillard).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of semi-structured interviews for studying how young people construct identities online.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: interviewer bias may still affect answers; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how young people construct identities online but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]
